verses.translation_literal: Give thanks to YHWH, for [he is] good, for for ever [is] his steadfast love.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give thanks to the LORD! Lift the voice, all of you, and say it plainly: he is good. And his steadfast love, his faithful love, has no end. It reaches past every horizon we can see.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a call to worship, shouted by a leader to a crowd, and the actors should play it as a summons, not a private reflection. The verb *hodu* is the imperative plural of *yadah*, which means to acknowledge out loud, to confess, to thank in public. Thanks here is spoken, never silent. The same words open Psalm 106, 107 and 136, so these are stock liturgical words that a crowd can pick up without being taught.

The KJV's 'mercy' is a poor fit for *chesed*. Mercy suggests a superior pardoning an offender, but *chesed* is loyalty owed inside a covenant, the faithfulness of a partner who keeps his word. The KJV also adds 'he is', which the Hebrew leaves out: it simply says 'for good', as a shout. The word *le'olam* is 'for the long age', not abstract eternity: time with no visible end. Note the doubled 'for' (*ki... ki...*): two reasons are stacked on top of each other, his goodness and his lasting loyalty.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, steadfast love: the faithfulness a party owes inside a bond. 'Mercy' (KJV) loses the covenant sense. The refrain recurs through the psalm (vv. 1-4, 29).
Hiphil imperative of yadah: to give thanks by speaking publicly, to acknowledge. It is a public act, not a feeling.

verses.translation_literal: Let Israel say, please, that for ever [is] his steadfast love.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let Israel say it now, the whole people together: his steadfast love has no end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The leader now hands the line to the crowd. The little word *na'* is a polite urging, 'please', 'I beg you', as when a cantor invites a congregation to answer. The KJV's 'now' catches the urgency but hides the courtesy, and YLT's 'I pray you' is closer. *Yomar* is singular, 'let Israel say', so the whole nation is spoken of as one voice answering in unison, as the Jerusalem pilgrims would.

This is the first of three responses. The list narrows from the nation to the priests to the God-fearers, as in Psalm 115:9-11 and 135:19-20. The actors should treat each as a new group stepping up to speak.

philological_notes.note: A particle of polite request, 'please', softening an imperative or jussive. The KJV renders it 'now'.

verses.translation_literal: Let them say, please, house of Aaron, that for ever [is] his steadfast love.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the house of Aaron say it too, the priests who tend the altar: his steadfast love has no end.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the priests answer. 'The house of Aaron' means the whole priestly family, the men who carry out the sacrifices and teach the people. Their answer carries more weight in the scene, because their daily work depends on the covenant that holds. The verb is plural (*yomeru*), where verse 2 was singular for Israel, since this is a group of individual officiants and not one national body. KJV's 'house of Aaron' is accurate here.

The medieval commentators read the verse through the story of David: Radak and Meiri link the priests to the massacre of Nob under Saul (1 Samuel 22), so that thanking God for the new reign would include thanks for the survival of the priesthood. That is their reading and the psalm does not say so, so it should be treated as an interpretation.

philological_notes.note: 'House of Aaron' is a standard phrase for the hereditary priesthood, as in Ps 115:10 and 135:19.

verses.translation_literal: Let them say, please, those who fear YHWH, that for ever [is] his steadfast love.
verses.translation_dramatic: And let all who stand in awe of the LORD say it: his steadfast love has no end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The third group is the widest. 'Those who fear YHWH' is not a class of officials. It names everyone who lives in reverent loyalty to him, and in the post-exilic setting it can include those from outside Israel who have joined themselves to the worshipping community. Fear in Hebrew is not terror but the awe that makes a person obedient. The KJV's 'them that fear the Lord' is sound; BBE's 'all worshippers' paraphrases the sense.

The fourfold call (all, Israel, Aaron, the God-fearers) is built to swell. Rashi reads the 'fearers' as the Levites; Radak and Meiri read them as the pious generally, and the actors should choose which crowd they have in mind.

philological_notes.note: 'Those who fear YHWH': the reverent, loyal worshippers. Here it forms a third group after Israel and Aaron's house. Rashi identifies them as the Levites; Radak takes them as the devout who devote themselves to wisdom.

verses.translation_literal: From the tight place I called Yah; Yah answered me in the wide-open place.
verses.translation_dramatic: Out of the narrow place I cried to the LORD. Walls pressed on every side. And the LORD answered me, and opened the ground beneath my feet until it ran wide.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the speaker, singular now, steps out of the crowd to tell a story in one line: from *metzar* to *merchav*. *Metzar* is a narrow gorge, a squeeze, the picture of distress as physical confinement; *merchav* is its opposite, an open broad space where a person can move and breathe. The two words are made to sound like a contrast, with the root *tzar* ('tight') set against *rachav* ('wide'). Ibn Ezra calls *merchav* the opposite of *metzar* and notes the repeated divine name as a rhetorical grace.

The KJV adds 'and set me in a large place', as though God placed the speaker there. The Hebrew says only that he answered 'in the wide place': the answer and the freedom come together. The poem also repeats the name *Yah*, the short form, at the start and at the end of the line, so the two names frame the answer like hands. In the shout of a festival crowd, 'Yah' would sound as a shorter, more intimate cry than the full name.

philological_notes.note: A narrow place, strait, distress. Set against merchav, 'a broad place', the pair describes distress as confinement and rescue as open space. Radak and Meiri note it is a noun of the doubled-root type.
A short form of the divine name YHWH, common in praise (as in hallelu-yah). It occurs twice in this verse.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH [is] for me; I will not fear. What can man do to me?
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is for me. I will not be afraid. What can any man do to me?
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker's confidence is short and flat, and should be played that way: four words, no ornament. *Yhwh li* means 'YHWH is for me', 'on my side', and in an ancient court or battle that is a legal and military statement: I have a patron who stands with me. The KJV's 'on my side' is good here. The Hebrew has no 'is', which makes it blunter still.

The last question, *mah ya'aseh li adam*, is rhetorical and the contrast is deliberate. *Adam* is a human being, a creature of earth (*adamah*), and the point is how small human power looks beside the divine. The same line is quoted in Hebrews 13:6. The verse sets up the next two, in which trusting man is called worse than taking refuge in God.

philological_notes.note: A human being, humankind, not a particular man; the word is related to adamah, 'ground'. The question stresses human weakness.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH [is] for me among my helpers, and I, I will look on those who hate me.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is for me, the first among all my helpers. And I will look, I myself, I will stand and watch as those who hated me fall.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two phrases carry the verse. *Be'ozerai* is literally 'in my helpers': the God is my helper, or among them, or as their leader. YLT's 'among my helpers' keeps the form; KJV's 'taketh my part with them that help me' reads it as God joining a team; BBE's 'my great helper' takes the plural as one of majesty. Ibn Ezra reports an older reading by Rabbi Moshe: God alone is enough against all helpers, since without him the others do not help at all.

The second half is tougher than English softens. *Er'eh be-sone'ai* is 'I will look at my haters', and the idiom means look with satisfaction on their defeat, as in Psalm 92:12. The KJV adds 'my desire' and ASV 'therefore', neither in the Hebrew. The pronoun *va'ani*, 'and I', is emphasised: it sets the speaker beside his helper and against the enemies.

philological_notes.note: 'In my helpers': the beth marks either 'among' or a beth of essence (YHWH is my help, in the role of helper). The plural may be one of majesty or may include human helpers. Ibn Ezra cites an older view that YHWH alone stands against all helpers.
'To look on' an enemy is an idiom for seeing him defeated, with satisfaction. Meiri compares Ps 92:12, 'my eye looked on my foes'.

verses.translation_literal: Good [is] to take refuge in YHWH, more than to trust in the human.
verses.translation_dramatic: Better, far better, to run for shelter to the LORD than to lean your whole weight on a man.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice drops from battle into plain proverb. The actors should play it as a lesson the speaker has paid for, not as a slogan. The grammar is a comparison: tov, 'good', followed by min on the second term, 'good ... more than', which is simply how Hebrew says 'better than'. The KJV's 'better' is right and so is every other English version here.

What the KJV does flatten is the pair of verbs. Chasah means to take refuge: it is the word for running under a wall, a rock or a wing, and it carries a physical picture of shelter from a storm or a pursuer. Batach means to rest your weight on something and feel secure. The KJV renders them 'trust' and 'put confidence', two soft abstractions, so the contrast between sheltering and merely leaning disappears. Rashi and Meiri both press this difference: refuge is shelter in someone's shadow, trust is reliance on something strong. The audience of a pilgrim hymn knew men of power were real shelter in their world, patrons, kings and treaty partners; the verse says even that is the lesser thing. The word adam, 'the human', stands for mortal humankind as such, and the next verse raises the stakes to the noble.

philological_notes.note: To take refuge: the picture is of going under something for cover (a wing, a shadow, a rock). It is more physical than the English 'trust'.
Min plus the infinitive: 'than trusting'. The min is the comparative of tov, so 'good ... than' means 'better than'. Batach is to rest one's weight on something and feel secure.

verses.translation_literal: Good [it is] to take refuge in YHWH, than to trust in nobles.
verses.translation_dramatic: Better to run for shelter to the LORD than to lean on the great, on princes and the open-handed.
verses.directors_commentary:
The line is repeated word for word, and only the last word changes: 'man' becomes 'nobles'. The speaker has just said that no human can be trusted, and now he moves up the social scale to the people one would most expect to be reliable. *Nedivim* are the generous, noble-minded, those of the ruling class, who by custom give gifts and protection. Malbim notes that the noble is the one whose nature is to give, and so the strongest case for trusting a man, and still the answer is no.

The KJV's 'princes' is a fair translation of the political sense. In a world of kings who make treaties and alliances, an audience living among kings, treaties and patrons would hear a warning against relying on any powerful protector.

philological_notes.note: Nobles, the generous, willing ones: people of high rank whose status expects giving. The root means 'to be willing, to give freely'. Ibn Ezra says they are the most honoured of men.

verses.translation_literal: All nations surrounded me; in the name of YHWH, for I will cut them off.
verses.translation_dramatic: All the nations ringed me round. But in the name of the LORD, in that name, I will cut them down.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone turns from proverb to battle. *Kol goyim* is 'all nations', the hostile foreign peoples as a whole, and the speaker is in the position of a besieged king or a besieged people. The singular 'me' lets one voice stand for a nation: Radak reads it of David and of Israel at once, Rashi of the final war of Gog and Magog.

The verb *amilam* is the hard word. The KJV's 'destroy' is vague, and the STEPBible 'fended off' is too soft. The root is *mul*, the verb of cutting that is also used for circumcision, so the Hebrew has the sound of a sharp stroke that cuts off, and some hear an echo of the nations as 'uncircumcised'. Rashi glosses it as 'cut them off' and links it to a wilting. The sound repeats in the verse's last word as a refrain (*amilam*), which the next two verses will bring back like a blow. The phrase 'in the name of YHWH' is the weapon: in the ancient world a name is the authority and the presence of the one who bears it.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil first person of mul: I cut them off. The same root is used for circumcision, which may add an echo. Rashi and Metzudat Zion connect it to cutting off and withering (compare yemolel in Ps 90:6). STEPBible 'I fended off' is weaker.
'In the name of YHWH': by his authority and presence. Metzudat David glosses it 'I will trust in the name of YHWH'.

verses.translation_literal: They surrounded me, yes, they surrounded me; in the name of YHWH, for I will cut them off.
verses.translation_dramatic: They surrounded me. Yes, they surrounded me, circle on circle, ring within ring. But in the name of the LORD I will cut them off.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first half is a stammer of dread: the same verb, *savvuni*, is said twice, once in a form with a doubled middle letter (*sabbuni*) and once with the full form (*sevavuni*). The effect is the same root twice, like a drum beat. Ibn Ezra compares the doubling in 'The LORD is my strength and my stronghold' and Meiri notes that the repetition is for emphasis. The actor should make the second one heavier than the first.

The KJV 'They compassed me about; yea, they compassed me about' reproduces the repetition well, and 'compassed' is archaic only in diction. The refrain of the second half repeats from the previous verse exactly. Malbim, with a later historical reading, takes the repetition as the three campaigns of Sennacherib against Judah; that is his reading, not the text's.

philological_notes.note: The same verb twice, in the contracted and then the full form, for intensity. Ibn Ezra compares it with repeated phrases elsewhere; Radak and Meiri call it a doubling for emphasis.

verses.translation_literal: They surrounded me like bees; they flickered out like a fire of thorns; in the name of YHWH, for I will cut them off.
verses.translation_dramatic: They swarmed round me like bees, a humming ring of stings. They blazed, and in a breath they were gone, like a fire in thorns that crackles up and dies. In the name of the LORD I will cut them off.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two similes with opposite speeds. The enemies come as bees: a dense, noisy, stinging cloud that fills the air. A swarm cannot be fought with a sword, and the fear is that of being surrounded by something small and many. Then, in the next phrase, the same enemies are a fire of thorns: dry thorn bushes burn high and fast, with a loud crackle, and leave no coals. Ibn Ezra says such a fire does not last, and Radak and Meiri add that it makes no embers.

The verb *do'akhu* is a passive that the English cannot copy cleanly: 'they were put out', 'they flickered out'. The KJV's 'quenched' is fine, but it misses the sound of the word. Rashi connects *da'akh* with a flame leaping from the wick. Metzudat Zion gives the same sense of springing away.

The KJV's 'for in the name of the Lord I will destroy them' is closer to the Hebrew than its rendering of verses 10 and 11, but it still says 'destroy' for *amilam*. This is the third and last of the refrains, and it should land as the climax.

philological_notes.note: They were extinguished, they flickered out. A verb used for lamps and fires. Rashi relates it to a flame leaping from the wick as it dies; Ibn Ezra glosses it 'were put out' as in 'his lamp goes out'.
Thorns, thornbushes: dry fuel that burns bright and fast but leaves no embers. Radak and Meiri stress that such a fire dies quickly and makes no coals.

verses.translation_literal: Pushing, you pushed me to fall, and YHWH helped me.
verses.translation_dramatic: You shoved me, you shoved me hard, shoved me to the very edge of falling. And the LORD — the LORD took hold of me and held me up.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker turns from describing the enemy to addressing him: 'you'. Rashi names the addressee outright, 'you, my enemy', and Radak and Meiri read the verse as spoken to the foe, so the actor should face the enemy for the first half and turn away from him on the second. After three verses of bees and thorn-fire, the image is bodily and close: a shove meant to topple a man.

The Hebrew opens with the infinitive absolute before the finite verb, dacho dechitani, 'pushing, you pushed'. It is the Hebrew way of intensifying the action, and it is why English versions say 'thrust sore', 'sorely' or 'violently'. Let the repeated root land twice, hard. The form lanpol, 'to fall', names the result the push aimed at; the KJV 'that I might fall' carries that sense well.

The release comes on a very short clause: vaYHWH azarani, 'and YHWH, he helped me'. The divine name is set first, ahead of the verb, so the helper arrives as the subject before the help is named. The KJV's 'but the Lord helped me' is faithful; the Hebrew has only 'and'.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive absolute before the finite verb of the same root: 'pushing, you pushed'. It intensifies the action; English cannot repeat the root without sounding stiff, so versions add 'sorely' or 'violently'.
'He helped me': the root also underlies the word 'helper' in verse 7, so the help promised there is the help given here.

verses.translation_literal: My strength and [my] song [is] Yah, and he has become to me for salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Yah is my strength, and Yah is my song. The one who held me up has become the rescue itself.
verses.directors_commentary: This line is borrowed whole: it is the refrain of the Song of the Sea (Exod 15:2) and also appears in Isa 12:2, so an audience would hear Israel's founding victory in it. Here the singer takes the Exodus words onto his own lips. The grammar is knotted: the yod on עזי and the construct-looking זמרת have given the commentators trouble (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri each argue it), and the traditional solution is that one suffix, 'my', serves both nouns, so 'my strength and song'. The KJV's "The Lord is my strength and song" captures it but supplies "The Lord" for the short divine name Yah and drops the verb-less abruptness of the Hebrew, where the two nouns come first and the name lands last. Note "song": it is a word for what you sing, and the commentators (Metzudat Zion) tie it to zemer, singing praise. Note also the tense: ויהי is a narrative 'and he became', Rashi's "and he became to me" where one might expect 'he was': the rescue has happened, and the strength has turned into the saving act. "For salvation" is literally 'into salvation', a becoming, not a mere helping.

philological_notes.note: 'Song' (or, on another reading, 'strength/choicest produce', as in Gen 43:11). The spelling looks like a construct form; the commentators resolve it by letting the suffix of עזי cover both nouns.
The short form of the divine name, YHWH, used in praise poetry and in the word hallelu-yah.

verses.translation_literal: The sound of a ringing shout and salvation [is] in the tents of the righteous: the right hand of YHWH does valour.
verses.translation_dramatic: Listen: from tent to tent, there is a sound, a ringing cry of joy, and it is the sound of rescue. In the camps of the righteous the singing has begun. The right hand of the LORD is doing mighty things.
verses.directors_commentary: The scene moves from the single man to the community: now we hear the neighbourhood. Tents (אהלים) are the ordinary homes of the people, and the noise coming out of them is רנה, a high, carrying shout of joy, the kind that goes up when a battle is won or a harvest comes in. The KJV's "tabernacles" is an archaism that makes modern ears think of the sanctuary; the Hebrew word is the plain word for a dwelling, and the poem's point is that the victory is celebrated in homes, not only in the temple. "Voice" in the KJV for קול is also correct but misleading: it is a noise, a sound, before it is a voice. The second half introduces the great refrain: the right hand, the hand of strength and action. "Doeth valiantly" (KJV) is good, but חיל is 'force, army, valour', so the phrase suggests an act of war. Radak links the cry in the tents with the actions of the right hand: when the hand wins, the tents sing. Malbim even hears the three occurrences as three stages of one victory. Direct the actors to hear the sound as a wave spreading through the camp.

philological_notes.note: A ringing cry of joy or a shout of triumph, louder and more public than 'singing'; the root also gives 'to cry out' in distress, so it is a sound that carries.
An idiom, 'to make/do strength', meaning to act with force, to win; חיל is also 'army', so the phrase has a martial sound. Metzudat Zion glosses חיל as 'strength and might'.

verses.translation_literal: The right hand of YHWH is raised high; the right hand of YHWH does valour.
verses.translation_dramatic: The right hand of the LORD, lifted high above the field. The right hand of the LORD, doing what only strength can do.
verses.directors_commentary: Repetition is the whole instrument of this verse: "the right hand of YHWH" opens both halves and echoes the end of the previous verse, so that it is said three times in a row. Ibn Ezra says the point of the threefold repeat is that this is something done again and again, "time after time"; Radak and Meiri say it is for strengthening. Treat it as a chant. The first half uses רוממה, 'is lifted up, raised high', in the sense of a hand held aloft over a victory or a standard raised; the KJV's "is exalted" is accurate but abstract, where the Hebrew picture is concrete, an arm upraised. In the ancient Near East the right hand is the hand of the weapon and of the oath, so a god's right hand is his power in action, and the image is Israelite as well as Egyptian and Mesopotamian in its use. For the actors: the first "right hand" is held up, the second drives forward.

philological_notes.note: A polel participle, 'is raised high / is exalted', which has a stronger, intensive form than the simple verb for 'rise'. Radak reads it as 'never faltering, as the hands of heroes and the generous do'.

verses.translation_literal: I will not die, for I will live, and I will recount the deeds of Yah.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will not die. I will live, and because I live I will tell it, every deed of the LORD, from the beginning to the end.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is built on two verbs that are exact opposites, אמות and אחיה, and a third that is the purpose of the other two: אספר, 'I will recount'. The singer says he lives in order to tell. This is a thought that runs through the Psalms: the dead cannot praise (Ps 115:17, a few verses before this one in the Hebrew Psalter), and so to be spared is to be given a task. Radak and Metzudat David read it as a defiant answer to the enemies who plotted his death; Malbim reads it as the voice of someone who was ill and recovered; Rashi hears Israel in exile. The KJV's "I shall not die, but live" is correct and famous, but the English "shall" hides the difference between a prophecy and a vow; the Hebrew imperfect can carry both. "Declare" is a little too formal for ספר, which is ordinary telling, the same root as 'counting' and as 'scribe' and 'book': to number off the deeds one by one. Play it quiet and certain, not shouted.

philological_notes.note: 'I will recount'. The root is the one for counting and for writing; to tell the deeds of Yah is to list them out one by one.
'The deeds of Yah', echoing the verb עשה used for the right hand's valour in the two verses before.

verses.translation_literal: Disciplining, Yah has disciplined me, but to death he has not given me.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD has corrected me, and corrected me hard. But he did not hand me over to death.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb is the same pattern as in verse 13: an infinitive absolute then a finite verb, יסר יסרני. And the pun is the point: after the enemy 'pushed, pushed', here it is the LORD who 'disciplines, disciplines'. The speaker places the same intensity in the hand of God as in the hand of the enemy, but with the opposite end. יסר is not 'to punish' but 'to discipline, train, correct' as a father does (the noun mussar is 'instruction'); the KJV's "chastened me sore" is good, if archaic, but 'chasten' has softened in English into 'to punish gently', whereas the Hebrew is severe and the cost is real. The second half is a legal and personal image: God did not 'give' (נתן) him over, as a prisoner is handed over to an executioner. The KJV's "given me over unto death" keeps that. Rashi reads the discipline as the exile, where his sins were paid; Radak says it was to cleanse him, not because God wanted to kill him. Metzudat David: the suffering is a cleansing, but he is not handed to his enemies. Play it as thanks with scars.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive absolute plus finite verb, 'disciplining, he disciplined me'. The root means to correct and train, not only to punish. Radak and Meiri explain the dagesh in the nun of יִסְּרַנִּי as 'for the beauty of the reading', like חָנֵּנִי.
'To death he did not give me': נתן with ל is to hand over to an authority or fate.

verses.translation_literal: Open to me the gates of righteousness; I will go in through them, I will give thanks to Yah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Open the gates for me, the gates of righteousness. Let me walk through them. I have a debt of thanks to the LORD, and I have come to pay it.
verses.directors_commentary: The poem now changes place: from the battlefield and the tents to the threshold of a building. A procession has arrived at a gate, and a single voice calls to the gatekeepers in the imperative plural, פתחו, 'open!' The gates are the temple gates, as Meiri, Metzudat David and Malbim all say; Radak reads it as a figure for words of praise. Anyone who has stood at a closed gate in an ancient city knows the tension: these gates may be refused to the unclean, and the entry liturgy of Ps 15 and 24 asks who may pass. The KJV's "gates of righteousness" is accurate; צדק is not abstract 'righteousness' but what is right, the gates where the right is done and declared, so the place is defined by its rightness. "Praise" in the KJV for אודה is too weak: the root ידה is to give public thanks, hands thrown out in acknowledgement. He does not come to ask but to give back. Malbim adds that the gates are called 'righteousness' because the deliverance came through discipline, by strict justice and not by grace alone.

philological_notes.note: 'The gates of righteousness': the temple gates, named for what is entered there. Meiri reads 'the gates of the house of praise and thanks'; Malbim says the king's own gate.
Hiphil of ידה: to acknowledge publicly, give thanks; the same root as Judah (יהודה) and as 'todah', the thank offering.

verses.translation_literal: This is the gate to YHWH; righteous ones will go in through it.
verses.translation_dramatic: This is the gate of the LORD. Those who are in the right will go in through it.
verses.directors_commentary: A second voice, from inside or beside the gate, answers the first. The Hebrew is blunt and verbless: זה השער ליהוה, 'this gate, to YHWH', where the lamed means it belongs to him or leads to him. The KJV's "This gate of the Lord" is a fragment that sounds like a sign, and in fact it is closer to what is spoken at a threshold: a gatekeeper's reply. The word צדיקים (the righteous) returns from verse 15, so the verse ties the tents to the temple: the people who sang in their homes now arrive at the door. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as the temple gate of those who come to give thanks; Radak and Meiri say it is the only gate through which praise may be offered, since praise belongs to God alone. In the ancient world a gate marks status: who may pass and who must wait. Say this line firmly, as a rule, not as an invitation.

philological_notes.note: The lamed of belonging or direction: 'to/for YHWH'. Whether the gate belongs to him or leads to him is open; both are possible.

verses.translation_literal: I will give thanks to you, for you answered me, and you have become to me for salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: I thank you. You answered me when I called, and you became my rescue.
verses.directors_commentary: Having crossed the threshold, the singer speaks the thanksgiving he promised in verse 19, and turns for the first time to address God directly: "you" (אודך) after many verses of speaking about him. The reason is given at once: כי עניתני, 'for you answered me'. The KJV's "heard me" is a softened rendering: ענה is 'to answer', a response, not just the act of hearing, which is the point, since he had called (v. 5) and was answered. The second half repeats verse 14's ויהי לי לישועה, now in the second person, ותהי: the same line, but spoken to God's face instead of about him. Ibn Ezra matches the two halves to the opening of the psalm: 'answered me' to 'answered me in the open space', 'salvation' to 'from the strait'. The English "praise" in the KJV and "art become" feel Elizabethan; keep the thanks plain and personal.

philological_notes.note: 'You answered me': ענה (B) is to respond or answer, and Metzudat Zion ties it to teshuvah, 'answer'. It is not the same root as 'afflict', although the spelling of the consonants is identical.

token_glosses.gloss: I will give thanks to you

verses.translation_literal: A stone the builders rejected has become the head of a corner.
verses.translation_dramatic: The builders looked at that stone and threw it aside. And that stone is now the head of the corner.
verses.directors_commentary: The most famous line of the psalm is a proverb, and its first image is of a worksite: builders sorting stones from a quarry heap and pushing aside the one that will not fit their plan. The Hebrew is short and has no articles on the stone or the corner: 'a stone ... head of a corner'. The KJV's "the head stone of the corner" adds the word 'stone' and a definiteness the Hebrew does not have; ראש פנה is literally 'the head of a corner', and scholars debate whether it means the cornerstone laid at the foundation or the capstone placed at the top of the angle. Metzudat David explains the custom: the best, most visible stone goes at the corner of the wall, showing on two sides. Who is the stone? Rashi says Israel, small among the nations; Ibn Ezra and Radak agree it may be Israel as a whole; Meiri adds David, the shepherd boy overlooked in 1 Sam 16:11; Malbim says Hezekiah. The Targum reads it as the boy Jesse's son, set aside by the builders. Keep the ambiguity: the actors do not need to decide who the stone is. מאס is stronger than the KJV's "refused": it is to reject with contempt, to find worthless.

philological_notes.note: 'They rejected': to reject as worthless or disgusting, a stronger verb than 'refuse' or 'put on one side'.
'Head of a corner': either a foundation cornerstone or a capstone at the angle of a wall; the Hebrew does not say 'stone' a second time.

verses.translation_literal: From beside YHWH this has come; it is wonderful in our eyes.
verses.translation_dramatic: This came from the LORD. And we, who see it, can only wonder.
verses.directors_commentary: The crowd answers the proverb. The change from 'I' to 'we' (בעינינו) is the signal: the individual voice that carried the psalm gives way to the community, and Rashi says "so will all of them say." The first phrase, מאת יהוה היתה זאת, is 'from beside YHWH has this come to be', the preposition mei-et giving a sense of source and presence at once. The KJV's "This is the Lord's doing" is idiomatic and good, but it turns a past event (היתה, 'it has come about') into a present statement, and it hides that the Hebrew puts the source first, so that 'from YHWH' is the first word the ear hears. Likewise "marvellous" for נפלאת is less than the Hebrew: the root פלא is the wonder that goes beyond understanding (Metzudat Zion links it to 'hidden, concealed', as in Judg 13:18), and the reaction is not applause but astonishment. Metzudat David: it is not by our hand and cannot be explained by nature. Say it half under the breath.

philological_notes.note: Niphal participle, 'is wonderful, beyond understanding'. Ibn Ezra notes the ending in tav stands for a feminine participle.
'From beside, from with': source together with presence. It is not the same as the simple 'from' (מן).

verses.translation_literal: This [is] the day YHWH has made; let us be glad and let us rejoice in it.
verses.translation_dramatic: This is the day. The LORD himself has made it. Let us be glad, let us rejoice in it.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse that became a song is built on two short commands, נגילה ונשמחה, 'let us be glad, let us rejoice', cohortative verbs in the first-person plural that invite the crowd to join in. The KJV's "we will rejoice and be glad" turns the invitation into a statement, and so loses the urging; the Hebrew is a call, not a report. The day in question is the day of the rescue and the procession: Radak says "the day of the salvation", Metzudat David "the day of that deliverance". It is not a general 'every day' or the Sabbath, though later readers sing it so. The verb עשה, 'made', has been in the poem all along (the deeds of v. 17, the right hand 'making' valour in vv. 15-16): the day is itself one of YHWH's deeds. Ibn Ezra offers another reading: the verbs lack an elided word, 'a day made for gladness'. The Hebrew order puts "made" before "YHWH", so the verb comes first, and the name arrives with the weight of a surprise. The last word, בו, 'in it', can mean in the day or in the deed. End the scene with the whole crowd in the gate, and give the last two verbs full voice.

philological_notes.note: Two verbs of gladness as cohortatives, 'let us exult and let us rejoice'. Metzudat Zion glosses נגילה as gilah and simchah, joy and gladness.
'YHWH has made': the verb comes before its subject. Radak takes 'made' to mean YHWH caused this day of salvation to come.

verses.translation_literal: I beg you, YHWH, save, please; I beg you, YHWH, grant success, please.
verses.translation_dramatic: Please, LORD, save us. Please. Please, LORD, let us succeed. Please.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two short cries, built as a matched pair, with every word doing the same work twice: an entreating particle, the name, a single imperative, a closing please. Hebrew: אָנָּא, YHWH, הוֹשִׁיעָה, נָּא // אָנָּא, YHWH, הַצְלִיחָה, נָּא. Only the verb changes, from rescue (הוֹשִׁיעָה, from יָשַׁע, to be brought out of a tight place into the open) to success (הַצְלִיחָה, from צָלַח, to push through, to break through and prosper). Play it as a crowd at the temple gate who have just heard that this is the day the LORD made: they ask for the deliverance first and the flourishing after, and each plea is sealed with the same small word. Radak hears Israel and the priests together praying for all who come to serve the LORD (Radak on Psalm 118:25); Malbim hears a double petition, rescue from the enemy and success in all their work from now on (Malbim on Psalm 118:25). Meiri takes it as the prayer of the days of the Messiah. The text itself names no speaker, so let the crowd voice it.

The KJV breaks the symmetry. It does render both אָנָּא ('I beseech thee') and both נָּא ('now'), but it moves them around: in the first line 'I beseech thee' sits after 'now' and before 'O Lord', while in the second it comes after 'O Lord'; 'now' follows 'Save' in the first line but follows 'send' in the second. The two lines, which are identical in build in Hebrew, therefore read differently in English. The KJV also adds the verb 'send' and the noun 'prosperity' for one Hebrew imperative, 'grant success', and puts in an 'I' where the Hebrew has no pronoun at all (ASV and BBE make it 'we'). Moreover 'now' in 'Save now' invites a modern reader to hear a time word, when נָּא is a particle of entreaty, closer to 'please' (YLT's 'I pray Thee' is nearer). Last, 'Save now' is הוֹשִׁיעָה נָּא, which is the Hebrew behind 'Hosanna'; the KJV Old Testament never lets a reader hear it.

philological_notes.note: An interjection of earnest entreaty, 'ah, please', a stronger and more urgent opening than נָּא alone. Here it opens both lines, so the verse is two prayers with the same urgency. It is not a plural and not a pronoun; 'I beseech thee' and 'we beseech thee' both add a subject the Hebrew leaves out.

Imperative of the Hiphil of יָשַׁע, 'bring into the open, rescue', with the entreating particle. The phrase is the source of 'Hosanna', the cry later taken up at a procession. In the verse it is an actual request for rescue, not yet an acclamation.

Imperative of the Hiphil of צָלַח, 'make succeed, grant breakthrough'. It is a verb, not the noun 'prosperity' of the KJV; the plea is that the LORD act so that what they do goes through, as in Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David, who gloss both verbs as 'now'.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [is] the one coming in the name of YHWH; we have blessed you from the house of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the LORD! Blessed — and we, standing here in the shadow of the LORD's own house, we have blessed you, and the blessing has come out to meet you from within its walls.
verses.directors_commentary:
A threshold verse: the crowd is at the gate, and someone is coming in. The Hebrew gives the greeting in two voices. The pilgrim is singular and the blessers are 'we', with a plural 'you' in בֵּרַכְנוּכֶם, so the line moves from one person coming to a whole group being welcomed. Ancient commentators split on who is speaking: Rashi has the greeting spoken to those bringing first-fruits and to pilgrims going up for the festivals; Malbim, reading it as a king's reception, hears the priests blessing the king as he arrives. The text itself does not say, and neither should the actors, who may simply play a ring of voices at the gate.

'In the name of YHWH' means on his authority, as his agent, not merely 'while saying his name'. The KJV's 'Blessed be he that cometh' reads as a wish; the Hebrew has no verb 'be', so it can equally be a statement, 'Blessed is he'. KJV also turns the perfect בֵּרַכְנוּכֶם into 'we have blessed you', which is right; but 'out of the house' hides מִבֵּית, 'from the house', the source from which the blessing flows, and that is the point: the temple is where blessing is stored and from where it is handed out. Later Christian ears hear the Palm Sunday crowd in the first half of the line, which is why the Gospels quote it.

philological_notes.note: A definite participle, 'the coming one', singular. It names no one; the identity of the arrival is left open, and the commentaries fill it in differently (pilgrim, offerer, king).
'In the name of YHWH': with his authority and under his protection. Malbim links it to the priestly blessing of Num 6:27, 'they shall put my name on the children of Israel'.
Piel perfect 1cp with a 2mp suffix, 'we have blessed you': a single word that carries subject, verb and object. The plural 'you' sets it apart from the singular הַבָּא before it.

verses.translation_literal: God [is] YHWH, and he gave light to us. Bind the festival with ropes, up to the horns of the altar.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is God — and he has given us light. Then bind the festival-offering with cords, and lead it on, up, until it stands at the horns of the altar.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two lines, two moods: a confession, then an order. 'God is YHWH' is the cry of people who have just been rescued and now say who did it. The KJV's 'God is the Lord, which hath shewed us light' dissolves the clause וַיָּאֶר לָנוּ ('and he lit up for us') into a relative clause. The Hebrew is more abrupt and more vivid: a statement, then a flare. Light here is deliverance and favor: compare the priestly 'may YHWH make his face shine on you' (Num 6:25). Malbim, imagining the temple procession met by torches, takes it more literally.

The second line is hard, and the KJV hides how hard. 'Bind the sacrifice with cords' supplies 'sacrifice'; the Hebrew says חַג, 'festival', the word for the pilgrimage feast and, by extension, for the offering brought at it. Rashi, Radak, Ibn Ezra and Meiri all take it to mean a festival animal tied with ropes and led to the altar; Ibn Ezra adds that the horns are the place where the blood is thrown. The Targum has a bound lamb. The alternative is the festival procession itself, 'bind' as in 'fasten' or 'tie on', with עֲבֹתִים taken as leafy boughs (the same noun describes thick-leaved trees); BBE reads 'let the holy dance be ordered with branches'. Neither reading is certain. The altar's 'horns' are the four raised corners of the stone block, the place of the most solemn contact between worshipper and God, a refuge for the hunted (1 Kings 1:50). The actors should know a living animal is being walked toward them, tied, nervous.

philological_notes.note: 'Festival, pilgrimage feast'; by extension the offering brought at one. Metzudat Zion explains that the offering is called ḥag because most offerings come at festivals. KJV 'sacrifice' is an interpretation, not a rendering.
Plural of עֲבֹת, thick twisted rope or cord; the same noun is used of leafy, interwoven boughs, which is why some read 'branches' here. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'thick ropes'.
The four projecting corners of the altar, onto which blood was put. Metzudat Zion calls them 'the projections at the top of the altar'; Ibn Ezra ties the horns to the throwing of blood.

verses.translation_literal: My God [are] you, and I will give thanks to you; my God, I will exalt you.
verses.translation_dramatic: You are my God — and I will thank you. My God — and I will lift you high, higher than my own voice can carry.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice drops from the crowd to one person. After the plural voices of the festival, the psalm returns to a single 'I' and 'my'; give the line to one actor, quiet and sure. Ibn Ezra notes that the psalm never tells us who speaks (the pilgrim, he suggests), which is a common poetic habit.

The KJV repeats 'thou art my God' in the second half ('thou art my God, I will exalt thee'), but the Hebrew does not: it says only 'my God, I will exalt you', and the verb is understood from the first half. This matters for the rhythm: a full statement, then a compressed echo, like a hand raised and a second gesture to finish it. The two verbs are also a pair of different acts. וְאוֹדֶךָּ comes from ידה, which means giving thanks and publicly confessing at once; אֲרוֹמְמֶךָּ from רום, 'be high', literally 'make you high'. KJV 'praise' for the first flattens the confessional side, which Radak hears when he says the speaker thanks God for the rescue 'in his mouth'.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of ידה, 'to give thanks, confess, acknowledge publicly'. It names a spoken act, thanksgiving as testimony, not an inner feeling. Malbim reads it as thanks for the good received, and the next verb as telling of the greater praises.
Polel of רום, 'to make high, to exalt'. The causative lifting is meant literally: the speaker raises God in speech above everything else.

token_glosses.gloss: and I will give thanks to you

verses.translation_literal: Give thanks to YHWH, for [he is] good; for his loyal love [is] for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give thanks to the LORD — for he is good. Give thanks, for his steadfast love has no end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends where it began (v. 1) with the refrain every pilgrim knew by heart; the whole crowd comes back in, and it should land as a release after the single voice of verse 28. Ibn Ezra hears the priests and Levites answering the speaker with this call to all.

The KJV 'his mercy endureth for ever' is a classic softening. 'Mercy' makes חֶסֶד sound like leniency granted from above; it means covenant loyalty, the steady faithfulness of a party that has bound itself and keeps its word. And 'endureth' is the translator's verb: the Hebrew has no verb, only לְעוֹלָם חַסְדּוֹ, 'for ever [is] his loyal love'. The two כִּי clauses ('for... for...') are not a single reason but two: he is good, and his loyalty is permanent. Staging: the crowd should be able to speak the line without being cued.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, steadfast love: the faithful kindness owed within a binding relationship and freely kept. English 'mercy' (KJV) and 'kindness' (YLT) each capture one side; no single English word holds all of it.
'For ever, to the distant horizon'. עוֹלָם names remote time with no visible end, not strict logical infinity; there is no verb 'endureth' in the Hebrew.
